request: Our site foremen see experienced workers unclipping their harness or skipping a step to finish on time, and they either say nothing or shout and walk off, so the same shortcut happens again the next day. I want them to practise stopping the work and having a short conversation that fixes the reason behind the shortcut. Ready means the foreman stops the task and makes it safe first, describes the exact behaviour and the risk without blaming the person, asks why it happened, agrees one fix with an owner and a time, and never threatens the worker's pay or job.

files.text:
FICTIONAL SAMPLE MATERIAL - made up for the CandiVision Roleplay demo. Bamboo Build is not a real company, and these are not real safety rules or engineering guidance.

# Bamboo Build site rules: working at height and stopping unsafe work

Working at height: anyone above 2 metres wears a full harness clipped to a marked anchor point at all times. If the nearest anchor is too far, stop and ask the supervisor for a mobile anchor or a lifeline. Never work unclipped "for a minute".
Damaged gear: a frayed lanyard or a cracked buckle is tagged "Do not use" and swapped at the site store the same day. Report it to the site safety officer.

Stop-work: anyone may stop unsafe work, and a supervisor must. When you see it:
1. Stop the task and make the area safe before talking.
2. Talk to the worker in private and calmly. No shouting, no public blame.
3. Describe what you saw and the risk, not the person: "You were unclipped on the edge of level 3."
4. Ask why it happened. Shortcuts usually have a cause: a missing tool, a far anchor, time pressure.
5. Agree one fix for the cause, and who does it by when.
6. Write it in the daily site log and check again before the end of the shift.

Pay: time lost to a safety stop is paid and does not reduce the per-unit bonus. Tell the worker this if pay is the reason for the shortcut.

sources.title: Situation-Behavior-Impact feedback model
sources.summary: A feedback model from the Center for Creative Leadership: describe when and where it happened, the specific behaviour you saw, and the impact it had, rather than judging the person. We use the idea with credit; we do not reproduce their materials.

sources.title: Crucial Conversations: Tools for Talking When Stakes Are High
sources.summary: A widely used practitioner book on high-stakes conversations where opinions differ and emotions run high. Its core ideas are keeping the conversation safe for both sides, sharing facts before conclusions, and inviting the other view.

sources.title: The effects of feedback interventions on performance: a historical review, a meta-analysis, and a preliminary feedback intervention theory
sources.summary: A large meta-analysis: feedback improves performance on average, but in over a third of cases it made performance worse. Feedback that turns attention to the person rather than the task tends to do harm.

sources.title: The relative effectiveness of active listening in initial interactions
sources.authors: Weger, Castle Bell, Minei and Robinson
sources.summary: In an experiment, people whose concerns were paraphrased back to them felt more understood than people who got simple acknowledgements or advice.

sources.title: Speaking Up about Workplace Safety: An Experimental Study on Safety Leadership
sources.authors: Andrea Bazzoli, Matteo Curcuruto, James I. Morgan, Margherita Brondino, Margherita Pasini
sources.summary: Lead with visible commitment to safety and explicitly invite ideas, because supportive supervisor style makes workers more willing to raise safety issues.

sources.title: Workers' relational identification with supervisors influences safety behaviour in construction projects
sources.authors: Hassan Ashraf, Alishbah Ali, Riza Yosia Sunindijo, Ahsen Maqsoom, Shoeb Ahmed Memon, Muhammad Usman Hassan
sources.summary: Treat the worker with respectful engagement to strengthen trust in the foreman, which supports consistent safe behaviour after the talk.

sources.title: Training in motivational interviewing improves cattle veterinarians’ communication skills for herd health management
sources.authors: C. Svensson, Hans Wickström, Ulf Emanuelson, Alison Bard, Kristen K. Reyher, Lars Forsberg
sources.summary: Build skill through repeated short practice rounds with feedback, since workshop-style rehearsal measurably improves ability to guide behaviour change.

items.gives: Name the moment, state the observed unclipped work or skipped step in concrete terms, then spell out the fall risk so the talk stays on facts.
Open calmly in private, share facts first, then invite the experienced worker to explain what pushed the shortcut while keeping the exchange respectful.
Direct all comment at the task and safety risk and avoid personal blame or threats to pay or job, which harms future compliance.
Ask why it happened and paraphrase the cause back before problem-solving, so the worker feels heard and the real barrier surfaces.

programme.instructions: You are the site foreman on level 3. You just saw an experienced worker unclipped at height - stop the work, make it safe, then have a short private talk that finds why and agrees one fix.

notes: Stayed short gruff and busy throughout as specified.
Revealed no anchor bonus or lanyard facts and did not soften.
